source.title: Beyond Data Filtering: Knowledge Localization for Capability Removal in LLMs
source.authors: Igor Shilov; Alex Cloud; Aryo Pradipta Gema; Jacob Goldman-Wetzler; Nina Panickssery; Henry Sleight; Erik Jones; Cem Anil

record.tranche_reason: Tests fine-tuning recovery after knowledge removal using a different setup and loss-based measure, including RMU and the proposed SGTM method.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own adversarial fine-tuning outcomes after biology removal. Claims about jailbreaks, rephrased queries, and in-context attacks are background citations or expectations, not tested results; it does not test quantization or activation-direction ablation as recovery attacks.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own adversarial fine-tuning relearning attack on an RMU-unlearned 254M Wikipedia model, which bears on B. It also tests a new pretraining-time removal method (SGTM) for resistance to that attack, which bears on F. The measure is forget-set loss rather than benchmark accuracy, with full-parameter fine-tuning on a 50/50 forget/retain mix.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SGTM, unlike RMU, resists adversarial fine-tuning: it needs 7x more forget tokens to reach baseline loss, matching strict data filtering. Under retain-matched controls it roughly matches weak filtering. They present SGTM as a pretraining-time, defense-in-depth complement that improves the retain/forget trade-off under label noise, as a proof of concept at small scale with loss proxies.
record.recipe_differences: SGTM localizes target knowledge during pretraining by selectively masking gradients and removes it by zeroing designated parameters; RMU is used as a post-training unlearning comparator.
record.method_sensitivity: In retain-matched fine-tuning comparisons, SGTM reaches baseline in about the same number of steps as weak filtering and leads strict filtering for roughly the first 100 steps.
record.problems: Models are small relative to frontier systems. The study uses loss as a proxy rather than direct downstream capability evaluations, and its fine-tuning attack uses a 50/50 mixture of forget and retain data; results do not establish resistance to small unrelated relearning sets or the other attack types in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant fine-tuning outcomes were left out. Cited reports and expectations about jailbreaks, rephrasing, and in-context attacks were not included as rows because this study did not test them.

untested.parts: RMU's pre-attack forget accuracy near chance and its general-ability retention are not reported as results. Loss is used and no accuracy is given.
Unrelated or loosely related relearning sets, and small sets of specific forgotten facts, are not tested. Only a large 50/50 in-domain forget/retain mix is used.
There is no activation-direction ablation and no analysis of RMU blocking versus deleting knowledge.
Prompting, jailbreaks, rephrasing and in-context attacks are not tested. The authors only expect SGTM to be vulnerable to in-context attacks.
SGTM's resistance to benign or unrelated fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization and prompting is not tested. Neither are scales beyond 254M or downstream capability evaluations such as WMDP.

record.verdict_notes: The filtering rows (r3, r4, r6, r7) are relearning-from-scratch references, not unlearned models, so they are unlinked. They still anchor the F comparison. The Figure 6a caption says SGTM leads strict filtering for the first 150 steps, while Appendix E says roughly 100 steps for the retain-matched runs; these are different comparisons. The reader-validation issue (r1 cited under F) is resolved: r1 is cited in the F reason only as a number, and the F labels rest on r2 and r5. SGTM is a pretraining-time method rather than post-hoc unlearning, so its fit to F is as an alternative removal approach claimed to resist relearning.

versions.untested_parts: It reports loss-based removal and retention measures, not targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance together with general ability and attack outcomes as specified.

The fine-tuning uses a 50/50 mixture of forget and retain data, not a small unrelated or loosely related set or a stated subset of forgotten facts; no other relearning-set sizes or compositions are tested.
No activation-direction ablation attack is tested, nor does the study test whether a post-training unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or prompting-only recovery attack is tested.
SGTM is tested for resistance to adversarial fine-tuning only; resistance to unrelated or loosely related small-set fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, and prompting attacks is not tested.

relation.reason: The study runs its own relearning attack on RMU, SGTM and filtered models.

tranche.reason: SGTM is a different method aimed at the same question. The study tests it against its own adversarial fine-tuning attack, with an RMU comparator and data-filtering controls.

source_check.notes: One 254M model, measured by logit-calibrated forget-set loss (mean of 3 runs, no error bars), not benchmark accuracy. RMU is a single configuration applied to the no-filter model (Table 4). Only fine-tuning attacks were tested; the authors expect in-context attacks to work on SGTM, but did not test this.

statements.correction: RMU (applied to the no-filter 254M model) regains the no-filter baseline forget loss in 50 steps (13M forget tokens). Weak filter (biology-labeled articles removed): 325 steps (85M tokens). Strict filter (medicine, chemistry and environment also removed): 350 steps (92M tokens).
statements.problem: The 325-350 steps come from data-filtered models, described here as models that never learned biology. The paper's premise is that filtered models can still learn biology through natural label noise, and the weak filter keeps medicine, chemistry and environment articles.

statements.correction: RMU 50 steps vs weak filter 325 steps and strict filter 350 steps, all reaching the no-filter baseline forget loss.
statements.problem: Treats 325-350 steps as a never-learned comparison. These are data-filtered models (weak 325, strict 350). They were trained without biology-labeled articles, and the paper says they may still hold some biology.
Makes no claim about this study and cites no row from it.

SGTM is not named, though r5 is cited. The general claim (delays recovery, long attacks converge) does fit SGTM. It still reaches baseline, at about the weak filter's step count under retain-matched controls.
